steps.title: Where to start: factor the modulus $1111$
steps.body: A huge power modulo a composite number is a signal to split the modulus into primes. Here $1111 = 11\cdot 101$, and both factors are prime. So we find $2^{1110}$ mod $11$ and mod $101$ separately with Fermat's little theorem ($a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ when $p$ is prime and does not divide $a$), then combine the two answers with the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

your_turn.answer: It is not divisible by $2$, $3$, $5$ or $7$, and $11^2 = 121 > 101$, so no larger prime needs checking.

steps.title: Work mod $11$
steps.body:
Fermat's little theorem with $p = 11$ gives $2^{10} \equiv 1 \pmod{11}$. Since $1110 = 10\cdot 111$, we get
$$2^{1110} = \left(2^{10}\right)^{111} \equiv 1^{111} = 1 \pmod{11}$$

your_turn.prompt: Check $2^{10} \equiv 1 \pmod{11}$ by hand: what is $2^5$ mod $11$, and then what is $2^{10}$ mod $11$?

steps.title: Work mod $101$
steps.body:
Fermat's little theorem with $p = 101$ gives $2^{100} \equiv 1 \pmod{101}$, so $2^{1100} = (2^{100})^{11} \equiv 1$. Since $1110 = 1100 + 10$, what is left is
$$2^{1110} = 2^{1100}\cdot 2^{10} \equiv 2^{10} \pmod{101}$$

your_turn.prompt: Find the remainder when $2^{10} = 1024$ is divided by $101$.

steps.title: Set up the combination
steps.body: We now need $n$ with $n \equiv 1 \pmod{11}$ and $n \equiv 14 \pmod{101}$. The numbers from $0$ to $1110$ that are $\equiv 14 \pmod{101}$ are $n = 14 + 101t$ for $t = 0, 1, \dots, 10$. We want the one that leaves remainder $1$ mod $11$.

your_turn.prompt: What are the remainders of $14$ and of $101$ when divided by $11$?

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: We need $3 + 2t \equiv 1 \pmod{11}$, so $2t \equiv -2 \equiv 9$; among $t = 0$ to $10$ only $t = 10$ works, since $2\cdot 10 = 20 \equiv 9$. Then $n = 14 + 1010 = 1024$. (Notice $1024 = 2^{10}$, which fits: we showed $2^{1110}$ and $2^{10}$ agree both mod $11$ and mod $101$.) The number $1111$ is $\equiv 0$, so it is not a second solution. The answer is **$1024$**.
